decks.title: Permutations and Combinations - Part 1: Counting, permutations and circular arrangements
goals: Apply the multiplication and addition principles and use factorial notation
Derive and use the number of permutations of r objects from n
Count arrangements with items together, never together, and numbers from digits
Count arrangements of letters with repeats and circular arrangements

slides.heading: Permutations and Combinations, Part 1
slides.body_md: Counting without listing: steps, orders, repeats and circles.

nodes.label: Permutations nPr and numbers from digits

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the multiplication and addition principles with factorials, permutations and numbers from digits, items always together or never together, arrangements with repeated letters, and circular permutations.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to the chapter on permutations and combinations. In this first part we learn the two counting principles, factorials, arrangements of different objects, restricted arrangements, words with repeated letters, and arrangements round a circle. Every count in this chapter was checked by listing small cases as well as by formula.

slides.heading: The multiplication principle
slides.body_md: If one task can be done in $m$ ways and, after it, a second task in $n$ ways, then the two tasks **together** can be done in $m \times n$ ways. The rule extends to any number of tasks.
bullets: A tree lists the outcomes: $3$ starters and $2$ drinks give $3 \times 2 = 6$ orders

visual.alt: Tree diagram: an order starts at the left, branches into three starters (soup, salad, wrap), and each starter branches into two drinks (tea, milk), giving six different orders at the leaves.
visual.caption: Three starters times two drinks gives six orders.

slides.narration: Suppose an order has a starter and then a drink. There are three starters, and each starter can go with either of two drinks. The tree shows six different orders. In general, when tasks follow one another and every task must be done, we multiply the numbers of ways.

slides.heading: Multiply or add?
slides.body_md: Use **multiplication** when tasks follow one another and all are done. Use **addition** when only one of several alternatives is done and the alternatives do not overlap.

rows: Tasks happen one after another; every task is done
Only one of several tasks is done; no overlap
Some choices are made in steps, others are alternatives
add the alternatives, then multiply by the steps

visual.alt: Table comparing the multiplication principle, used when tasks follow one another, with the addition principle, used when only one of several alternative tasks is done, with a combined example of four shirts and three trousers or two shorts.
visual.caption: And means multiply; or means add.

slides.narration: Ask yourself whether the word is and or the word is or. And means the tasks follow one another, so multiply. Or means only one alternative is used, so add. Many problems mix both, as with shirts, and then trousers or shorts. Add the alternatives first, then multiply by the steps.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a code
slides.body_md: A code has two letters from P, Q, R, S, T (letters may repeat) followed by two **different** digits from $1$ to $9$. How many codes are there?

rows: any of P, Q, R, S, T

visual.alt: Worked example 1 table: a code with two letters from five, repeats allowed, then two different digits from one to nine; the choices are 5, 5, 9 and 8, so the number of codes is 1800.
visual.caption: Count place by place.

slides.narration: Count place by place. Each of the two letters has five choices, because letters may repeat. The first digit has nine choices, and the second digit has eight, because it must differ from the first. Multiplying gives one thousand eight hundred codes.

slides.heading: Factorial notation
slides.body_md: $n! = n(n - 1)(n - 2) \cdots 3 \times 2 \times 1$, so $n! = n \times (n - 1)!$. We define $0! = 1$ so that this rule works at $n = 1$.

visual.alt: Table of factorials from 0 factorial to 8 factorial: 1, 1, 2, 6, 24, 120, 720, 5040 and 40320, each checked as n times the previous factorial, with 0 factorial defined as 1.
visual.caption: $n! = n \times (n - 1)!$, and $0! = 1$.

slides.narration: The factorial of n is the product of the whole numbers from n down to one. So n factorial equals n times the factorial of n minus one. At n equal to one this rule gives one factorial equals one times zero factorial, which is why we define zero factorial to be one.

slides.heading: Quick check: dividing factorials
slides.body_md: Decide whether a quotient of factorials behaves like a quotient of numbers.
slides.narration: Write out the products before you cancel.

slides.heading: Permutations of r objects from n
slides.body_md: An arrangement of $r$ objects chosen from $n$ different objects is a **permutation**. Fill the places in order: $n$ choices, then $n - 1$, and so on.

visual.alt: Table of slots for arranging 4 of 9 different objects: the choices for the first to fourth place are 9, 8, 7 and 6, and for general n and r they are n, n minus 1, n minus 2, down to n minus r plus 1, giving 3024 for n equal to 9 and r equal to 4.
visual.caption: Each place has one choice fewer than the one before.

slides.narration: To arrange r objects from n different objects, fill the places one after another. The first place has n choices, the second has one fewer, and the last place, the r th, has n minus r plus one choices. Multiplying gives n factorial divided by n minus r factorial. When r equals n we get n factorial.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: office-bearers
slides.body_md: A club has $11$ members. In how many ways can a president, a secretary and a treasurer be chosen?
bullets: The roles are different, so order matters

rows: president, secretary, treasurer: the order of the $3$ roles matters

visual.alt: Worked example 2 table: choosing a president, a secretary and a treasurer from 11 members is an ordered choice of three from eleven, so the number of ways is 11 times 10 times 9, which is 990.
visual.caption: Different roles mean order matters.

slides.narration: The three roles are different, so choosing Asha as president and Bala as secretary is different from the other way round. So this is a permutation of three from eleven. That is eleven times ten times nine, which is nine hundred and ninety.

slides.heading: Forming numbers from digits
slides.body_md: Fill the **restricted place first**: the units place for even numbers or multiples of $5$, the first place when $0$ is among the digits.

headers: Digits $1$ to $5$, three places, no repeat
rows: one fewer choice for the first place only

visual.alt: Table of rules for forming numbers from digits: fill the restricted place first. For three-digit numbers from the digits 1 to 5 without repetition there are 60 in all, 24 even and 36 greater than 300.
visual.caption: Restricted places first, then the rest.

slides.narration: When forming numbers, deal with the restricted place first. For an even number, choose the units digit first. For a number above a given value, choose the first digit first. If zero is available, the first digit cannot be zero. Then fill the remaining places in order.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: numbers above 6000
slides.body_md: How many four-digit numbers greater than $6000$ can be formed from the digits $2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9$ if no digit is repeated?

rows: must be $6$, $7$ or $9$ (the digits $2$, $4$ and $5$ give numbers below $6000$)

visual.alt: Worked example 3 table: four-digit numbers above 6000 from the digits 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9 without repetition; the first digit is 6, 7 or 9, the other three places use the remaining five digits in order, 60 ways, so there are 180 numbers.
visual.caption: Fill the first place, then arrange the rest.

slides.narration: The thousands digit must be six, seven or nine, so there are three choices. After that, the other three places take any of the five remaining digits, in order, which is sixty ways. So there are three times sixty, one hundred and eighty, numbers.

slides.heading: Quick check: a permutation value
slides.body_md: Evaluate a permutation as a product of consecutive factors.
slides.narration: Start at nine and write three factors going down.

slides.heading: Items always together or never together
slides.body_md: **Together:** glue the items into one block, arrange the units, then arrange inside the block. **Never together:** subtract the together count from the total.

nodes.label: Always together: glue the items into one block

visual.alt: Flow for restricted arrangements: glue the items that must be together into one block, arrange the resulting units, multiply by the arrangements inside the block, and for never together subtract the together count from the total.
visual.caption: Block for together; complement for never together.

slides.narration: When some items must stay together, treat them as a single block. Arrange the units, then multiply by the ways to arrange the items inside the block. When items must never be together, count all arrangements and subtract the arrangements in which they are together.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: two captains apart
slides.body_md: Nine players stand in a line. In how many lines are the two captains **not** next to each other?

rows: block and $7$ others: $8! = 40320$ units orders, times $2$: $80640$

visual.alt: Worked example 4 table: nine players stand in a line; all lines number 362880; the two captains together number 2 times 8 factorial, which is 80640; so the lines with the captains never together number 282240.
visual.caption: Subtract the together case from the total.

slides.narration: There are nine factorial lines in all, three hundred and sixty two thousand eight hundred and eighty. When the captains are together, we have a block and seven other players, eight units, in eight factorial ways, times two orders inside the block. Subtracting leaves two hundred and eighty two thousand two hundred and forty.

slides.heading: Arrangements with alike letters
slides.body_md: Swapping two equal letters gives the same arrangement. Divide by the factorial of each group of alike letters.
bullets: The word sees has six distinct arrangements, not twenty four

visual.alt: Table listing all six distinct arrangements of the letters of SEES: EESS, ESES, ESSE, SEES, SESE and SSEE, which equals 4 factorial over 2 factorial times 2 factorial.
visual.caption: Six, not $4! = 24$: swapping equal letters changes nothing.

slides.narration: Take the four letters of the word sees, with two s and two e. If all four were different there would be twenty four arrangements. But swapping the two s letters changes nothing, and neither does swapping the two e letters. The list shows only six distinct arrangements.

slides.heading: The rule for repeated letters
slides.body_md: If $p$ letters are alike of one kind and $q$ of another, the number of distinct arrangements of $n$ letters is $\dfrac{n!}{p!\,q!}$.

visual.alt: Table of the rule for arrangements with alike letters: all different letters give n factorial, and each group of p alike letters divides the count by p factorial; SEES has four letters with two alike pairs, giving 6 arrangements.
visual.caption: Divide by the factorial of each group of alike letters.

slides.narration: The rule is simple. Start with n factorial, then divide by p factorial for the group of p alike letters, and by q factorial for the group of q alike letters, and so on for each group. For the word sees, four factorial over two factorial times two factorial gives six.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a word with three S
slides.body_md: Find the number of distinct arrangements of the letters of SUCCESS, and the number with the three S's together.

rows: SUCCESS has $7$ letters: S three times, C twice, U once, E once
units SSS, U, C, C, E: $\dfrac{5!}{2!} = 60$

visual.alt: Worked example 5 table: the word SUCCESS has 7 letters with S three times and C twice, so 7 factorial over 3 factorial times 2 factorial, 420, arrangements; with the three S together the count is 5 factorial over 2 factorial, 60.
visual.caption: Group alike letters into blocks before dividing.

slides.narration: The word has seven letters, with s three times and c twice. So the number of distinct arrangements is seven factorial divided by three factorial times two factorial, which is four hundred and twenty. With the three s letters glued into one block, there are five units, with c twice, giving five factorial over two factorial, which is sixty.

slides.heading: Circular permutations
slides.body_md: Round a table, turning everyone one place gives the **same** arrangement. Fix one object and arrange the other $n - 1$: there are $(n - 1)!$ circular arrangements.

visual.alt: Six people A, B, C, D, E and F seated round a circular table in the clockwise order A, B, C, D, E, F; turning the whole seating by one place gives the same circular arrangement.
visual.caption: Rotating all six seats leaves the circular arrangement unchanged.

slides.narration: When people sit round a circular table, there is no first seat. Turning everyone round by one place gives the same arrangement. So we fix one person in place, and arrange the other n minus one people in n minus one factorial ways.

slides.heading: Clockwise and anticlockwise
slides.body_md: If clockwise and anticlockwise orders are **different** (people at a table) the count is $(n - 1)!$. If they are the **same** (beads, garland, key ring) the count is $\dfrac{(n - 1)!}{2}$.
bullets: Four people: $3! = 6$ round a table; $3$ if mirror images are the same

visual.alt: Table of the six circular arrangements of four people A, B, C and D with A fixed: ABCD, ABDC, ACBD, ACDB, ADBC and ADCB read clockwise, each shown with its mirror image read the other way; mirror images pair up into three.
visual.caption: Fix A: $3! = 6$ circular arrangements; $3$ if mirror images are the same.

slides.narration: Here are the six circular arrangements of four people with a fixed. Each is shown with its mirror image, the same circle read the other way. For people at a table, these are different. For a necklace that can be turned over, a circle and its mirror image are the same, so we halve the count and get three.

slides.heading: Circular count summary
slides.body_md: First decide whether the circle can be turned over. Then count: $(n-1)!$ or $\dfrac{(n-1)!}{2}$. Compare with $n!$ in a row.

headers: Number of arrangements of $n$ different objects
rows: clockwise and anticlockwise are different (people at a table)
clockwise and anticlockwise are the same (beads, garland, key ring)

visual.alt: Table of circular permutations of n different objects: n minus 1 factorial when clockwise and anticlockwise orders differ, half of that when they are the same as for a necklace, compared with n factorial in a row; for seven objects 720, 360 and 5040.
visual.caption: Fix one object to remove the rotations.

slides.narration: Always decide whether the circle can be turned over. For people at a table, use n minus one factorial. For a necklace, a garland or a key ring, use n minus one factorial divided by two. The count in a row is n factorial, which is larger.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: a bracelet
slides.body_md: A bracelet is made from $8$ different charms and can be turned over. Find the number of bracelets, and the number with two named charms next to each other.

rows: Bracelet of $8$ different charms, can be turned over
Two named charms next to each other
block and $6$ others: $(7 - 1)! = 720$, times $2$ orders, halved for turning over: $\dfrac{2 \times 720}{2} = 720$

visual.alt: Worked example 6 table: a bracelet of eight different charms that can be turned over can be made in 5040 over 2, which is 2520, ways; with two named charms side by side the count is 2 times 720 halved, which is 720.
visual.caption: Circular count first, then halve for turning over.

slides.narration: Eight different charms on a bracelet that can be turned over give seven factorial divided by two, which is two thousand five hundred and twenty. With two named charms side by side, glue them into one unit. Seven units round a circle give six factorial, times two orders for the pair, and then we halve for turning over, which gives seven hundred and twenty.

slides.heading: Quick check: table or row
slides.body_md: Compare a seating round a table with a seating in a row.
slides.narration: Remember what turning the whole table does.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Multiply for steps, add for alternatives; $n! = n(n-1)!$ and $0! = 1$
Together: block; never together: subtract; fill restricted places first
Repeated letters divide by $p!\,q!$; circles use $(n-1)!$, halved if turning over is allowed

nodes.label: Multiply for steps, add for alternatives; $n! = n(n-1)!$

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: multiply for steps and add for alternatives with factorials, the permutation formula, block and complement methods for together and never together, and the rules for repeated letters and circular arrangements.
visual.caption: Part 1 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. Multiply for steps, add for alternatives. The number of permutations of r from n is n factorial over n minus r factorial. For restricted arrangements, use blocks for together and subtraction for never together. Repeated letters divide by factorials. Circles use n minus one factorial, halved if the circle can be turned over.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Say whether order matters before choosing a formula
Fill the restricted place first when forming numbers
For never together, write total and together as separate lines
For circles, state whether turning over is allowed

headers: How ISC marks are usually given
rows: restricted place filled first 1, other places 1, total 1
block or total 1, inside arrangements 1, subtraction 1
count of letters and repeats 1, division 1, each condition 1

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 1: permutation evaluations, numbers from digits, together and never together, letters of a word and circular arrangements each earn marks for the formula or restricted place, the other places and the final total.
visual.caption: Name the method, show each factor.

slides.narration: In the examination, say whether order matters before you choose a formula. When forming numbers, fill the restricted place first. For never together, write the total and the together count on separate lines. For circles, state clearly whether the circle can be turned over.

decks.title: Permutations and Combinations - Part 2: Combinations, selections and mixed problems
goals: Derive nCr from nPr and use its properties
Solve equations such as nC8 = nC6 and nP2 = 156
Count selections with conditions and selections of alike things
Solve mixed problems of selecting and arranging

slides.heading: Permutations and Combinations, Part 2
slides.body_md: Selecting without order, with conditions, and then arranging.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: combinations and their properties, selections with conditions such as at least or included, selections of alike things, counting diagonals and triangles, and mixed problems of selecting and arranging.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to the second part. Here the order no longer matters. We meet combinations, their properties, selections with conditions, selections of alike things, counting diagonals and triangles, and mixed problems where we select first and then arrange.

slides.heading: From permutations to combinations
slides.body_md: A **combination** is a selection in which order does not matter. Each selection of $r$ objects can be arranged in $r!$ ways, so $^{n}P_{r} = r! \times {}^{n}C_{r}$.

visual.alt: Flow deriving the combination formula: choose r of n objects in nCr ways, arrange each choice in r factorial ways, so nPr equals r factorial times nCr, and nCr equals n factorial over r factorial times n minus r factorial.
visual.caption: Selections times arrangements gives permutations.

slides.narration: A combination is a selection where order does not matter. Each selection of r objects can be arranged in r factorial ways. So the number of permutations is r factorial times the number of combinations. Dividing, the number of combinations equals n factorial over r factorial times n minus r factorial.

slides.heading: Selections and arrangements
slides.body_md: From A, B, C, D choose $2$: there are $6$ selections but $12$ arrangements, since each selection has $2! = 2$ orders.

headers: Selection of $2$ from A, B, C, D

visual.alt: Table listing the six selections of two letters from A, B, C and D, AB, AC, AD, BC, BD and CD, each with its two arrangements, giving 12 arrangements in all, which is 2 factorial times 4C2.
visual.caption: $6$ selections, $12$ arrangements: $^{4}P_{2} = 2! \times {}^{4}C_{2}$.

slides.narration: Here are the six selections of two letters from a, b, c and d. Each selection has two arrangements, so there are twelve arrangements altogether. That is two factorial times six. This is the link between permutations and combinations.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: using symmetry
slides.body_md: Evaluate $^{13}C_{10}$.

visual.alt: Worked example 1 table of Part 2: 13C10 equals 13C3 by symmetry, which is 13 times 12 times 11 over 6, giving 286.
visual.caption: Swap to the smaller lower number.

slides.narration: Choosing ten from thirteen is the same as choosing the three to leave out. So thirteen choose ten equals thirteen choose three. Then thirteen times twelve times eleven over six gives two hundred and eighty six.

slides.heading: Properties and Pascal's triangle

visual.alt: Pascal triangle table for n from 0 to 8, each row built by adding the two numbers above it; for example row 8 is 1, 8, 28, 56, 70, 56, 28, 8, 1, and 56 plus 70 equals 126, the entry of row 9.
visual.caption: Each entry is the sum of the two above: $^{8}C_{3} + {}^{8}C_{4} = {}^{9}C_{4}$.

slides.narration: There are two key properties. First, choosing r is the same as leaving out n minus r, so the two combinations are equal. Second, Pascal's rule says that two neighbouring entries in a row add to the entry below them. If two combinations with the same n are equal and the lower numbers differ, the lower numbers add up to n.

slides.heading: Quick check: a symmetry
slides.body_md: Decide whether two combinations of ten objects are equal.
slides.narration: Think of choosing what to leave behind.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: finding n

rows: lower numbers differ, so they add up to $n$: $n = 7 + 4$

visual.alt: Worked example 2 table of Part 2: nP2 equal to 156 gives n times n minus 1 equal to 156, so n is 13; nC7 equal to nC4 means the lower numbers add up to n, so n is 11.
visual.caption: Reject negative roots; $n$ is a positive integer.

slides.narration: For the first equation, n times n minus one equals one hundred and fifty six. This gives n squared minus n minus one hundred and fifty six equals zero, which factorises to n minus thirteen times n plus twelve. Since n is positive, n is thirteen. For the second, the lower numbers differ, so they add up to n, giving eleven.

slides.heading: Selections with conditions
slides.body_md: A named object **included**: reduce both $n$ and $r$ by $1$. **Excluded**: reduce $n$ only. **At least** one: use the complement or split into cases.

headers: Condition (team of $4$ from $5$ men and $4$ women)
rows: choose the other $3$ from the remaining $8$: $^{8}C_{3}$

visual.alt: Table of selection conditions for a team of four from five men and four women: no condition gives 126, a named man included 56, excluded 70, at least one woman 121, and at most one woman 45.
visual.caption: Included: reduce $n$ and $r$. Excluded: reduce $n$. At least: use the complement or cases.

slides.narration: Conditions change the numbers in the formula. If a named person must be in, choose the rest from the others, so both the pool and the number to choose go down by one. If the person must be out, only the pool goes down. For at least one, subtract the none case from the total, or add up the cases.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: at least two women
slides.body_md: A team of $4$ is chosen from $7$ men and $5$ women with at least $2$ women. Find the number of teams.

visual.alt: Worked example 3 table of Part 2: a team of four from seven men and five women with at least two women has cases of 2, 3 or 4 women giving 210, 70 and 5 teams, a total of 285.
visual.caption: Split by the number of women, then add.

slides.narration: Split by the number of women. With two women and two men there are two hundred and ten teams. With three women and one man, seventy. With four women, five. Adding gives two hundred and eighty five teams.

slides.heading: Selections of alike things
slides.body_md: From $p$ alike things you can take $0, 1, \ldots, p$: that is $p + 1$ choices. Different things are taken or left: $2$ choices each. Multiply, then subtract the empty selection.

rows: $p$ alike of one kind, $q$ alike of another
$0$ to $p$ and $0$ to $q$, minus the empty selection

visual.alt: Table of the number of selections of at least one item from alike things: n alike things give n selections; p alike and q alike give p plus 1 times q plus 1 minus 1; r different things give 2 to the r minus 1; combined groups multiply, for example 5 alike and 4 alike give 29.
visual.caption: Alike things: count how many to take. Different things: take or leave.

slides.narration: When things are alike, only the number taken matters. From p alike things, you can take none, one, up to all p, which is p plus one choices. Different things are each taken or left, which is two choices each. Multiply the choices for each group, and remove the empty selection if at least one item must be taken.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: fruit and sweets
slides.body_md: A basket holds $5$ identical apples, $4$ identical oranges and $3$ different sweets. In how many ways can at least one item be taken?

visual.alt: Worked example 4 table of Part 2: five identical apples, four identical oranges and three different sweets; the choices are 6, 5 and 8, which multiply to 240, and removing the empty selection leaves 239.
visual.caption: Subtract the empty selection last.

slides.narration: There are six choices for the apples, five for the oranges, and two to the power three, which is eight, for the sweets. Multiplying gives two hundred and forty, including taking nothing. Removing that one leaves two hundred and thirty nine.

slides.heading: Quick check: identical stickers
slides.body_md: Count the outcomes when the objects are identical.
slides.narration: Only the number taken makes a difference.

slides.heading: Diagonals of a polygon
slides.body_md: Joining pairs of vertices of a convex polygon gives $^{n}C_{2}$ segments; $n$ of them are sides. So the diagonals number $^{n}C_{2} - n = \dfrac{n(n-3)}{2}$.

visual.alt: A convex heptagon ABCDEFG with its 7 sides drawn solid and its 14 diagonals dashed: of the 21 segments joining pairs of vertices, 7 are sides.
visual.caption: A heptagon: $21$ segments, $7$ sides, $14$ diagonals.

slides.narration: A convex polygon with n vertices has n choose two segments joining pairs of vertices. Of these, n are the sides. The remaining segments are the diagonals. The picture shows a heptagon with seven sides drawn solid and fourteen diagonals dashed.

slides.heading: Counting triangles and lines
slides.body_md: Any three vertices form a triangle: $^{n}C_{3}$. If $m$ of the points are collinear, subtract $^{m}C_{3}$ triangles; lines drop by $^{m}C_{2} - 1$.

visual.alt: Table of geometry counts: a convex polygon with n sides has nC2 segments, n(n minus 3) over 2 diagonals and nC3 triangles from its vertices; if m of n points are collinear the triangles number nC3 minus mC3, for example 55 for n 8 and m 3.
visual.caption: Subtract the collinear triples.

slides.narration: Any three points that are not in a line form a triangle. So the number of triangles is n choose three, minus the number of choices of three from the m collinear points. For lines, the m collinear points give one line instead of m choose two, so subtract m choose two and add one.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: points with a line
slides.body_md: Eight points are marked and exactly three of them are collinear. Find the number of triangles and of distinct straight lines.

rows: $8$ points; exactly $3$ of them, $(1,1)$, $(3,3)$, $(5,5)$, are on one line

visual.alt: Worked example 5 table of Part 2: eight points with exactly three on one line give 56 minus 1, which is 55, triangles, and 28 minus 3 plus 1, which is 26, distinct straight lines.
visual.caption: Three collinear points give one line, not three.

slides.narration: Eight points give fifty six choices of three, but one of them is the collinear triple, which makes no triangle. So there are fifty five triangles. For lines, there are twenty eight pairs, but the three collinear points give three pairs and only one line, so twenty eight minus three plus one is twenty six lines.

slides.heading: Mixed problems: select, then arrange
slides.body_md: When a task needs both a selection and an arrangement, **select first** with combinations, **then arrange** with a factorial or circular count, and multiply.

nodes.label: Read the task: which objects, how many?
Arrange: use $r!$ or a circular count
Multiply the stages and check a small case

visual.alt: Flow for mixed problems: read the task, select the objects with combinations for each group, arrange them with a factorial or circular count, then multiply the stages and check a small case.
visual.caption: Select first, arrange second.

slides.narration: Mixed problems have two stages. First select the objects, using combinations for each group. Then arrange them, using a factorial or a circular count. The total is the product of the stages. Checking a small case with a list is a good habit.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: five-letter words
slides.body_md: Five-letter words use $3$ of $5$ consonants and $2$ of $4$ vowels, all letters different. How many words are there?

visual.alt: Worked example 6 table of Part 2: five-letter words from five consonants and four vowels with three consonants and two vowels; 10 consonant selections times 6 vowel selections times 120 arrangements give 7200 words.
visual.caption: Select each group, then arrange the whole set.

slides.narration: Select first. Choosing three of five consonants gives ten ways, and choosing two of four vowels gives six ways. That is sixty sets of letters. Then arrange each set of five letters in one hundred and twenty ways. The total is seven thousand two hundred words.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: a committee at a round table
slides.body_md: Four of $7$ people are chosen and seated round a circular table. Find the number of ways.

sections.heading: 1. Counting principles and factorials
sections.body_md:
**Multiplication principle:** if a task has $k$ steps that can be done in $m_1, m_2, \ldots, m_k$ ways one after another, the whole task can be done in $m_1 m_2 \cdots m_k$ ways. **Addition principle:** if only one of several non-overlapping tasks is done, add the counts.

The **factorial** of a positive integer is $n! = n(n - 1)(n - 2) \cdots 2 \times 1$, so $n! = n \times (n - 1)!$, and $0! = 1$ by definition. Factorials cancel by writing the larger one down to the smaller: $\dfrac{8!}{5!} = 8 \times 7 \times 6$.

key_terms.definition_md: Successive independent steps: multiply the numbers of ways.

sections.heading: 2. Permutations and numbers from digits
sections.body_md:
A **permutation** is an arrangement of objects in order. The number of arrangements of $r$ objects chosen from $n$ different objects is $^{n}P_{r} = n(n - 1) \cdots (n - r + 1) = \dfrac{n!}{(n - r)!}$, derived by filling $r$ places in turn. In particular $^{n}P_{n} = n!$.

For numbers made from digits, fill the **restricted place first**: the units place for even numbers and multiples of $5$, the first place when $0$ is available. Digits may or may not repeat; say which.

key_terms.definition_md: An ordered arrangement of selected objects.
A place with a condition, filled before the others.

sections.heading: 3. Items together or never together
sections.body_md:
**Always together:** glue the $k$ items into one block, arrange the $n - k + 1$ units in $(n - k + 1)!$ ways, then arrange inside the block in $k!$ ways. **Never together:** all arrangements minus the arrangements with the items together. For two items in a row of $n$: $n! - 2 \times (n - 1)!$.

The same ideas apply to letters of a word: block the vowels, or place the consonants first and put the vowels in the gaps.

sections.heading: 4. Arrangements with alike things
sections.body_md:
If $p$ of $n$ letters are alike of one kind, $q$ alike of a second kind and $r$ alike of a third, the number of **distinct** arrangements is $\dfrac{n!}{p!\,q!\,r!}$. Equal letters swapped give the same arrangement, so divide by each group's factorial.

For conditions such as "the three S's together", form the block first, then divide only for repeats left among the remaining units. Check a small word by listing, for example SEES has $\dfrac{4!}{2!\,2!} = 6$ arrangements.

sections.heading: 5. Circular permutations
sections.body_md:
In a circle there is no first place, so a rotation gives the same arrangement. Fix one object: the other $n - 1$ can be arranged in $(n - 1)!$ ways when clockwise and anticlockwise orders are **different** (people at a table). When they are **the same** (necklace, garland, key ring, bracelet) the count is $\dfrac{(n - 1)!}{2}$.

For two items together round a table treat them as a unit: $2 \times (n - 2)!$ arrangements of $n$ people. For alternating groups, seat one group first, then place the other in the gaps.

key_terms.definition_md: An arrangement round a circle in which rotations count as the same.

sections.heading: 6. Combinations and their properties
sections.body_md:
A **combination** is a selection in which order does not matter. Each selection of $r$ objects can be arranged in $r!$ ways, so $^{n}P_{r} = r! \times {}^{n}C_{r}$ and $^{n}C_{r} = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n - r)!}$.

Properties: $^{n}C_{r} = {}^{n}C_{n - r}$; $^{n}C_{r - 1} + {}^{n}C_{r} = {}^{n + 1}C_{r}$ (Pascal's rule); and if $^{n}C_{a} = {}^{n}C_{b}$ with $a \ne b$ then $a + b = n$. Selections from alike things: $p$ alike give $p + 1$ choices; with $q$ alike and $r$ different, the selections of at least one item number $(p + 1)(q + 1)2^{r} - 1$.

sections.heading: 7. Conditions, geometry and mixed problems
sections.body_md:
With a team of $r$ from $n$: a named object **included** gives $^{n-1}C_{r-1}$; **excluded** gives $^{n-1}C_{r}$; **at least one** of a kind: total minus none, or split into cases.

A convex polygon with $n$ sides has $^{n}C_{2} - n = \dfrac{n(n - 3)}{2}$ diagonals. Three points not on a line give a triangle: $^{n}C_{3}$, less $^{m}C_{3}$ when $m$ points are collinear.

For mixed problems, **select first** with combinations for each group, **then arrange** with a factorial or a circular count, and multiply the stages.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How ISC marks are usually awarded**
- *Evaluation and equations (2-3 marks):* the formula, the simplified product, the value; for equations, the quadratic and the rejection of invalid roots.
- *Numbers from digits (3 marks):* the restricted place first, the other places, the product.
- *Together or never together (3-5 marks):* the block or total, the inside arrangements, the subtraction.
- *Letters of a word (3-5 marks):* the number of letters and each repeat, the division, each condition.
- *Circular arrangements (2-3 marks):* the base count $(n - 1)!$, the condition, the final number.
- *Selections and committees (3-5 marks):* each case, the products, the sum.
- *Section D (5 marks):* questions come in parts such as 1 + 1 + 1 + 2; label each part.

**Common mistakes**
- Using $^{n}P_{r}$ when order does not matter, or $^{n}C_{r}$ when it does.
- Forgetting the $k!$ arrangements inside a block of $k$ items.
- Subtracting only one together case for never together (two items can be together in $2 \times (n - 1)!$ ways).
- Dividing by factorials of letters that are not repeated.
- Using $n!$ round a circle, or forgetting to halve when the circle can be turned over.
- Counting the empty selection when at least one item must be taken.
- Treating identical objects as if they were different.

questions.stem_md: By the definition used in factorial notation, the value of $0!$ is

options.text_md: not defined

questions.solution_md: The rule $n! = n \times (n - 1)!$ at $n = 1$ gives $1! = 1 \times 0!$, and since $1! = 1$ we need $0! = 1$. The values $0$ and $-1$ would break this rule, and the factorial is defined at $0$, so it is not undefined.

questions.stem_md: For a positive integer $n$, the quotient $\dfrac{(n + 2)!}{n!}$ simplifies to
questions.solution_md: Write $(n + 2)! = (n + 2)(n + 1)\,n!$ and cancel $n!$ to get $(n + 1)(n + 2)$. The expression $n(n + 1)$ is what $\dfrac{(n + 1)!}{(n - 1)!}$ gives, and $n + 2$ cancels only one factor.

questions.stem_md: An imagined study app lets a learner choose one of $6$ avatars, one of $5$ colour themes and one of $3$ sound packs. The number of different set-ups is
questions.solution_md: The three choices are made one after another and independently, so by the multiplication principle there are $6 \times 5 \times 3 = 90$ set-ups. The value $14$ adds the numbers of options, which is the rule for alternatives, not for successive choices; $30$ ignores the sound pack; $45$ halves the product for no reason.

questions.stem_md: For a school event Rohan, an imagined student, wears one of $4$ shirts together with either one of $3$ pairs of trousers or one of $2$ pairs of shorts, never both. The number of different outfits is
questions.solution_md: The bottoms are alternatives, so there are $3 + 2 = 5$ choices (addition principle). The shirt is chosen as well, so the outfits number $4 \times 5 = 20$. The value $24$ multiplies all three counts, as if he wore trousers and shorts together; $9$ adds everything; $14$ pairs the shirts with the trousers only and then adds the $2$ shorts.

questions.stem_md: The number of ways of arranging $3$ of $8$ different trophies in a row on a display shelf is the value of $^{8}P_{3}$, which is
questions.solution_md: $^{8}P_{3} = 8 \times 7 \times 6 = 336$. The value $56$ is $^{8}C_{3}$, which ignores the order of the three trophies; $24$ is $8 \times 3$; and $6720$ is $\dfrac{8!}{3!}$, which has too many factors.

questions.stem_md: The positive integer $n \ge 3$ that satisfies $^{n}P_{3} = 10 \times {}^{n}P_{2}$ is
questions.solution_md: $^{n}P_{3} = n(n - 1)(n - 2)$ and $^{n}P_{2} = n(n - 1)$. Dividing by $n(n - 1)$ (non-zero) leaves $n - 2 = 10$, so $n = 12$. The value $10$ forgets the $-2$, and $13$ and $8$ do not satisfy the equation.

questions.stem_md: Four-digit numbers greater than $5000$ are formed from the digits $2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8$, no digit being used twice. The number of such numbers is
questions.solution_md: The thousands digit must be $5, 6, 7$ or $8$, which gives $4$ choices. The other three places take any of the remaining $6$ digits in order: $^{6}P_{3} = 120$. So there are $4 \times 120 = 480$ numbers. The value $840$ ignores the condition, and $864$ allows repeated digits.

questions.stem_md: Five-digit numbers with five different digits are made from the digits $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7$. The number of such numbers is
questions.solution_md: The first digit cannot be $0$, so it has $7$ choices. The remaining four places are filled from the other $7$ digits (which include $0$): $^{7}P_{4} = 840$. The total is $7 \times 840 = 5880$. The value $6720$ is $^{8}P_{5}$, which allows a leading zero; $11760$ lets the remaining places choose from $8$ digits.

questions.stem_md: The number of distinct arrangements of all the letters of the word ARRANGE is
questions.solution_md: There are $7$ letters with the letter A twice and the letter R twice. The number of distinct arrangements is $\dfrac{7!}{2!\,2!} = 1260$. The value $5040$ treats all letters as different, and $2520$ divides for only one repeated letter.

questions.stem_md: Seven imagined students sit in a row on a long bench. Three particular students insist on sitting next to one another. The number of seatings is
questions.solution_md: Glue the three students into one block: the block and the other $4$ students make $5$ units, arranged in $5! = 120$ ways. Inside the block the three can swap in $3! = 6$ ways. The total is $120 \times 6 = 720$. The value $4320$ counts $6$ units instead of $5$, and $120$ forgets the order inside the block.

questions.stem_md: Eight different flags are hung in a line from left to right. Two particular flags must never hang side by side. The number of ways to hang the flags is
questions.solution_md: Count all hangings and remove those with the two flags together. All: $8! = 40320$. Together: glue them to make $7$ units, $7! = 5040$ ways, times $2$ orders, which is $10080$. So $40320 - 10080 = 30240$. The value $35280$ forgets the factor $2$, and $10080$ is the number with the flags together.

questions.stem_md: Eight different people take seats round a circular table, and two seatings that differ only by a rotation are the same. The number of different seatings is
questions.solution_md: Fix one person to remove the rotations; the other $7$ can then be seated in $7! = 5040$ ways. The value $40320$ counts rotations as different, and $2520$ would also treat a seating and its mirror image as the same, which is not asked here.

questions.stem_md: Nine beads, all different, are threaded on a thin wire to form a necklace that can be turned over, so a pattern and its mirror image count as one. The number of different necklaces is
questions.solution_md: Round a ring there are $(9 - 1)! = 40320$ arrangements. A necklace can be flipped, which pairs each arrangement with its mirror image, so the count is halved: $\dfrac{8!}{2} = 20160$. The value $40320$ does not halve; $362880$ and $181440$ treat the beads as in a row.

questions.stem_md: The number of ways of choosing $12$ cards from $15$ different cards, the order of choosing being ignored, is $^{15}C_{12}$, which equals
questions.solution_md: $^{15}C_{12} = {}^{15}C_{3} = \dfrac{15 \times 14 \times 13}{3 \times 2 \times 1} = 455$. The value $2730$ is $^{15}P_{3}$ and does not divide by $3!$; $1365$ is $^{15}C_{4}$; and $180$ is $15 \times 12$.

questions.stem_md: If $^{n}C_{9} = {}^{n}C_{5}$, the value of $n$ is
questions.solution_md: Two combinations with the same $n$ are equal when the lower numbers are equal or add up to $n$. Since $9 \ne 5$, $n = 9 + 5 = 14$. The value $4$ subtracts instead of adding; $45$ multiplies; $13$ is an off-by-one slip.

Pascal's rule $^{n}C_{r-1} + {}^{n}C_{r} = {}^{n+1}C_{r}$ with $n = 14$, $r = 6$ gives $^{15}C_{6} = 5005$. Direct check: $2002 + 3003 = 5005$. The value $3003$ is $^{15}C_{5}$, from a wrong lower number; $6006$ doubles the larger term; $1001$ is unrelated.

questions.stem_md: A quiz team of $4$ is chosen from $5$ boys and $4$ girls of an imagined class so that it contains at least one girl. The number of possible teams is
questions.solution_md: Remove from all teams the teams with no girl. All teams: $^{9}C_{4} = 126$. All-boys teams: $^{5}C_{4} = 5$. So the answer is $126 - 5 = 121$. The value $126$ includes the all-boys teams; $224$ picks a girl first and then three others, which counts a team with two girls twice or more; $116$ is not a count of this kind.

questions.stem_md: A drawer holds $4$ identical pens and $3$ identical pencils. The number of ways of taking at least one of these writing tools from the drawer is
questions.solution_md: The number of pens taken can be $0, 1, 2, 3, 4$, which is $5$ choices, and pencils $0, 1, 2, 3$, which is $4$ choices, so $5 \times 4 = 20$ selections including taking nothing. Remove that one: $20 - 1 = 19$. The value $20$ keeps the empty selection; $12 = 4 \times 3$ forgets that none may be taken; $7$ adds the numbers of tools.

questions.stem_md: Ten points are marked on a map of an imagined park. Exactly four of them lie on one straight path and no other three are in a line. The number of triangles with three of these points as vertices is
questions.solution_md: Any $3$ points give $^{10}C_{3} = 120$ selections, but three points on the path do not form a triangle. Those number $^{4}C_{3} = 4$. So there are $120 - 4 = 116$ triangles. The value $120$ keeps the flat triples; $114$ subtracts $^{4}C_{2} = 6$, the number of pairs; $112$ is not obtained from any correct step.

questions.stem_md: Five-letter words, meaningful or not, are made from $4$ vowels and $6$ consonants, all different, using no letter twice. Exactly $2$ vowels must appear. The number of such words is
questions.solution_md: First select: $^{4}C_{2} \times {}^{6}C_{3} = 6 \times 20 = 120$ sets of $5$ letters. Then arrange each set: $5! = 120$ ways. Total $120 \times 120 = 14400$. The value $120$ stops after the selection; $1200$ divides by $2!\,3!$ as if the letters repeated; $172800$ orders the letters twice.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The letters of the word LEVEL can be arranged in $30$ different ways.

**Reason (R):** When $n$ things are arranged in a row and $p$ of them are alike of one kind and $q$ alike of another kind, the number of distinct arrangements is $\dfrac{n!}{p!\,q!}$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: LEVEL has $5$ letters, with L twice and E twice, so $\dfrac{5!}{2!\,2!} = 30$ and A is true. R is the general rule used for it, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The number of ways of choosing $3$ different books from $8$ different books is $56$.

**Reason (R):** For $0 \le r \le n$, $^{n}C_{r} = r! \times {}^{n}P_{r}$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: $^{8}C_{3} = \dfrac{8 \times 7 \times 6}{6} = 56$, so A is true. R is false: the correct relation is $^{n}P_{r} = r! \times {}^{n}C_{r}$, because each selection can be ordered in $r!$ ways. For $n = 8$, $r = 3$, R would give $6 \times 336$, not $56$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A convex polygon with $10$ sides has $45$ diagonals.

**Reason (R):** A convex polygon with $n$ sides has $^{n}C_{2} - n$ diagonals.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true: of the $^{n}C_{2}$ segments joining two vertices, $n$ are sides. For $n = 10$ this gives $45 - 10 = 35$ diagonals, so A is false; the number $45$ is the number of segments joining pairs of vertices, sides included.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both values equal $126$, so A is true, and R is a correct formula. But R does not explain the equality: that comes from $^{n}C_{r} = {}^{n}C_{n-r}$, since choosing $4$ of $9$ is the same as leaving out $5$ of $9$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** From $5$ different fruits a child can take some or all in $31$ ways (at least one fruit).

**Reason (R):** Each fruit is either taken or left, so there are $2^{5}$ selections, and removing the empty one leaves $2^{5} - 1$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: $2^{5} - 1 = 31$, so A is true, and R gives exactly that count by the multiplication principle: two options for each of the $5$ fruits, less the empty selection. R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Seven people sit round a table and two particular people must sit side by side. The number of seatings is $2 \times 6! = 1440$.

**Reason (R):** When two persons must be together, treat them as one unit and multiply by the $2!$ orders inside the pair.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: R is the correct method, but A uses it wrongly. The pair and the other $5$ people make $6$ units, which are placed round the table in $(6 - 1)! = 120$ ways, not $6!$. With the $2!$ orders inside the pair the number is $2 \times 120 = 240$, so A is false.

questions.stem_md: The quotient $\dfrac{8!}{4!}$ equals $2!$, because $8$ divided by $4$ is $2$.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: Factorials do not divide like numbers. $\dfrac{8!}{4!} = 8 \times 7 \times 6 \times 5 = 1680$, which is far from $2! = 2$.

questions.stem_md: Six different guests can be seated round a circular table in the same number of ways as they can be seated in a straight row of six chairs.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: In a row there are $6! = 720$ seatings. Round a table the rotations of a seating are the same, so there are only $(6 - 1)! = 120$. The two numbers differ by a factor of $6$.

questions.stem_md: For choosing from ten different tokens, the number of ways to take $3$ of them equals the number of ways to take $7$ of them.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: Choosing $3$ tokens to take is the same as choosing the $7$ to leave behind, so $^{10}C_{3} = {}^{10}C_{7} = 120$.

questions.stem_md: Picking $2$ of $6$ different books to lend to a friend, and arranging $2$ of the $6$ on a shelf in a particular order, are counted by the same number.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: Lending is a selection: $^{6}C_{2} = 15$. Arranging is an ordered choice: $^{6}P_{2} = 30$. Each pair of books can be put on the shelf in $2!$ ways, so the second number is twice the first.

questions.stem_md: If a child may take any number of $6$ identical stickers, but at least one, the number of different outcomes is $6$.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: Because the stickers are identical, an outcome is fixed only by how many are taken: $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ or $6$. That is $6$ outcomes. (The $2^6 - 1 = 63$ count applies only when the stickers are all different.)

questions.stem_md: The value of $^{9}P_{3}$ is ____.
A convex octagon has ____ diagonals.
questions.solution_md: Joining pairs of the $8$ vertices gives $^{8}C_{2} = 28$ segments, of which $8$ are sides, so there are $28 - 8 = 20$ diagonals.

questions.stem_md: The value of $\dfrac{12!}{10!\,2!}$ is ____.
The letters of the word BANANA can be arranged in ____ distinct ways.
questions.solution_md: There are $6$ letters with A three times and N twice: $\dfrac{6!}{3!\,2!} = \dfrac{720}{12} = 60$.

questions.stem_md: Seven different keys are fixed on a ring that can be turned over, so two arrangements that are mirror images are not counted separately. The number of different key rings is ____.
questions.solution_md: Round a ring there are $(7 - 1)! = 720$ arrangements, and turning the ring over pairs them up, so there are $\dfrac{720}{2} = 360$.

questions.stem_md: How many odd three-digit numbers with three different digits can be written using only the digits $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7$?
questions.solution_md: The units digit is odd: $4$ choices ($1, 3, 5, 7$). The hundreds digit is not $0$ and not the units digit: $8 - 2 = 6$ choices. The tens digit is any of the $8 - 2 = 6$ digits left. The number is $4 \times 6 \times 6 = 144$.

marking_scheme.step: Units digit: $4$ choices (fill the awkward place first)

questions.stem_md: Find the number of distinct arrangements of all the letters of the word PARALLEL.
questions.solution_md: PARALLEL has $8$ letters: A twice, L three times, and P, R, E once each. The number is $\dfrac{8!}{2!\,3!} = \dfrac{40320}{12} = 3360$.

questions.stem_md: A debating club of an imagined school has $7$ boys and $6$ girls. A team of $5$ is formed with exactly $2$ girls. In how many ways can the team be chosen?
questions.solution_md: Choose the girls and the boys separately and multiply. Girls: $^{6}C_{2} = 15$. Boys: $^{7}C_{3} = 35$. The number of teams is $15 \times 35 = 525$.

questions.stem_md: Seven imagined friends sit round a circular table, and two of them have quarrelled and must not sit next to each other. Seatings that differ by a rotation are the same. Find the number of seatings.
questions.solution_md: All seatings: $(7 - 1)! = 720$. Seatings with the two together: treat them as one unit, so $6$ units round the table in $5! = 120$ ways, times $2$ orders, which is $240$. So the number is $720 - 240 = 480$.

questions.stem_md: The ratio of the number of ways of choosing $3$ objects from $2n$ different objects to the number of ways of choosing $3$ from $n$ different objects is $11 : 1$. Determine the integer $n$.
Using factorials, prove that $^{n}C_{r} = {}^{n}C_{n-r}$ for $0 \le r \le n$, and explain the result in words.

answer.model_answer_md: $^{n}C_{n-r} = \dfrac{n!}{(n - r)!\,\bigl(n - (n - r)\bigr)!} = \dfrac{n!}{(n - r)!\,r!} = {}^{n}C_{r}$. In words: choosing $r$ objects to take is the same decision as choosing the $n - r$ objects to leave, so the two counts are equal. For example $^{9}C_{3} = {}^{9}C_{6} = 84$.

questions.solution_md: Replace $r$ by $n - r$ in the factorial formula and the two denominators swap.

marking_scheme.step: Substitute $n - r$ in $\dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n - r)!}$ and simplify

questions.stem_md: Determine the value of $n$, a positive integer, that makes $(n + 1)! = 12 \times (n - 1)!$ true.
questions.solution_md: Expand the larger factorial down to the smaller one and cancel.

questions.stem_md: A coach picks the first five batters, in batting order, from a squad of nine imagined players. In how many different ways can the batting order be picked?

answer.model_answer_md: The order matters, so this is $^{9}P_{5} = 9 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6 \times 5 = 15120$.

questions.solution_md: An ordered choice of $5$ from $9$ is a permutation.

questions.stem_md: In how many distinct arrangements of the letters of the word ENGINE do the two E's stand side by side?

answer.model_answer_md: Treat the two E's as one block EE. The units are EE, N, G, I, N: $5$ units with N twice. The number of arrangements is $\dfrac{5!}{2!} = 60$. (All arrangements of ENGINE number $\dfrac{6!}{2!\,2!} = 180$.)

questions.solution_md: Glue the alike letters into one block, then allow for the other repeated letter.

questions.stem_md: Six different flowers are strung into a garland that can be turned over. In how many different ways can the garland be made?

answer.model_answer_md: Round a ring there are $(6 - 1)! = 120$ arrangements. A garland can be turned over, so each arrangement and its mirror image are one design: $\dfrac{120}{2} = 60$.

questions.solution_md: Circular count first, then halve for turning over.

questions.stem_md: Find the value of $r$ for which $^{14}C_{r} = {}^{14}C_{r+4}$.

answer.model_answer_md: Equal combinations with the same $n$ need $r + (r + 4) = 14$, because $^{n}C_{a} = {}^{n}C_{b}$ with $a \ne b$ means $a + b = n$. So $2r = 10$ and $r = 5$. Check: $^{14}C_{5} = {}^{14}C_{9} = 2002$.

questions.solution_md: Use $^{n}C_{a} = {}^{n}C_{b} \Rightarrow a + b = n$ when $a \ne b$.

questions.stem_md: Verify by evaluating each term that $^{11}C_{4} + {}^{11}C_{5} = {}^{12}C_{5}$.

answer.model_answer_md: $^{11}C_{4} = \dfrac{11 \times 10 \times 9 \times 8}{24} = 330$ and $^{11}C_{5} = \dfrac{11 \times 10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7}{120} = 462$. The sum is $792$. Also $^{12}C_{5} = \dfrac{12 \times 11 \times 10 \times 9 \times 8}{120} = 792$, so the two sides are equal.

questions.solution_md: This is Pascal's rule with $n = 11$ and $r = 5$.

questions.stem_md: A panel of $3$ is to be chosen from $8$ volunteers, among whom are Zoya and Ravi (imagined people). Zoya must be on the panel and Ravi must not be. In how many ways can the panel be chosen?

answer.model_answer_md: Zoya is in and Ravi is out, so the other $2$ places are filled from the remaining $8 - 2 = 6$ volunteers: $^{6}C_{2} = \dfrac{6 \times 5}{2} = 15$.

questions.solution_md: Fix the forced member, remove the excluded one, then choose the rest.

marking_scheme.step: Remaining pool is $6$ and the places left are $2$

questions.stem_md: Three-digit numbers below $300$ are written using only the digits $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$, and a digit may be used more than once. How many such numbers are there?

answer.model_answer_md: The hundreds digit must be $1$ or $2$: $2$ choices. The tens and units digits are each any of the $5$ digits. By the multiplication principle the number is $2 \times 5 \times 5 = 50$.

questions.solution_md: Handle the restricted place first.

questions.stem_md: Four-digit numbers are written using only the digits $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$, and a digit may be used more than once. Find how many such numbers (a) there are in all, (b) are multiples of $5$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The first digit cannot be $0$: $6$ choices. Each of the other three digits has $7$ choices. The number is $6 \times 7 \times 7 \times 7 = 2058$.

(b) A multiple of $5$ ends in $0$ or $5$: $2$ choices for the units digit. Then $6 \times 7 \times 7 \times 2 = 588$.

questions.solution_md: Count the restricted places first: the first digit and the units digit.

questions.stem_md: The seven different letters of the word MACHINE are arranged in a row. Find the number of arrangements (a) in all, (b) in which the three vowels are together, (c) that begin with a vowel and end with a consonant.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $7! = 5040$.

(b) Treat the three vowels A, I, E as one block: the block and the $4$ consonants make $5$ units, $5! = 120$ ways, and the vowels can be ordered inside in $3! = 6$ ways. The number is $120 \times 6 = 720$.

(c) The first place has $3$ vowel choices, the last has $4$ consonant choices, and the middle five places take the other $5$ letters in $5! = 120$ ways: $3 \times 4 \times 120 = 1440$.

questions.solution_md: Block method for (b); fill the end places first for (c).

questions.stem_md: Six imagined friends sit round a circular table, and two seatings that differ only by a rotation are the same. Find the number of seatings (a) in all, (b) with two particular friends side by side, (c) with those two friends not side by side.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $(6 - 1)! = 120$.

(b) Treat the two friends as one unit: $5$ units round the table in $(5 - 1)! = 24$ ways, and the pair can swap in $2$ ways: $2 \times 24 = 48$.

(c) Subtract: $120 - 48 = 72$.

questions.solution_md: Circular count with the pair as one unit; subtract for the complement.

questions.stem_md: A garden committee of $5$ is chosen from $6$ men and $5$ women of an imagined housing society. Find the number of committees (a) with no restriction, (b) with exactly $3$ women, (c) with at least $4$ women.
questions.solution_md: Split by the number of women, then add the cases for (c).

questions.stem_md: Explain why $^{n}P_{r} = r! \times {}^{n}C_{r}$, and use $^{9}C_{4} = 126$ to find $^{9}P_{4}$.

answer.model_answer_md: Each selection of $r$ objects from $n$ can be arranged in a row in $r!$ ways, and different selections give different arrangements, so the number of arrangements is $^{n}P_{r} = r! \times {}^{n}C_{r}$. For $n = 9$ and $r = 4$: $^{9}P_{4} = 4! \times 126 = 24 \times 126 = 3024$. Check: $9 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6 = 3024$.

questions.solution_md: Select first, then order the selection.

marking_scheme.step: Each selection can be ordered in $r!$ ways

questions.stem_md: A craft box holds $4$ identical red marbles, $3$ identical blue marbles and $2$ different stickers. Find the number of ways of taking at least one of these items.

answer.model_answer_md: Red marbles: $0$ to $4$ taken, $5$ choices. Blue marbles: $0$ to $3$, $4$ choices. Each sticker is taken or left, $2 \times 2 = 4$ choices. All selections: $5 \times 4 \times 4 = 80$. Remove the case where nothing is taken: $80 - 1 = 79$.

questions.solution_md: Identical items give $(p + 1)$ choices; each different item gives $2$; subtract the empty selection.

questions.stem_md: A convex polygon has $54$ diagonals. (a) Find the number of its sides. (b) Find the number of triangles that can be formed by joining three of its vertices.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) With $n$ sides the diagonals number $^{n}C_{2} - n = \dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2} - n = \dfrac{n(n - 3)}{2}$. Setting $\dfrac{n(n - 3)}{2} = 54$ gives $n^2 - 3n - 108 = 0$, so $(n - 12)(n + 9) = 0$ and $n = 12$.

(b) Any $3$ vertices form a triangle: $^{12}C_{3} = 220$.

questions.solution_md: Diagonals are all pairs of vertices minus the sides.

questions.stem_md: Four-letter words, meaningful or not, are made from $3$ different vowels and $5$ different consonants, using no letter twice. Each word has exactly $2$ vowels and $2$ consonants. Find the number of such words.

answer.model_answer_md: Select the letters: $^{3}C_{2} \times {}^{5}C_{2} = 3 \times 10 = 30$ sets of $4$ letters. Arrange each set in $4! = 24$ ways. The number of words is $30 \times 24 = 720$.

questions.solution_md: Select the vowels and the consonants, then arrange every selected set.

questions.stem_md: Four boys and four girls of an imagined dance group sit round a circular table so that boys and girls alternate. Two seatings that differ only by a rotation are the same. Find the number of seatings.

answer.model_answer_md: Seat the $4$ boys first round the table: $(4 - 1)! = 6$ ways. This leaves $4$ gaps, one between each pair of neighbouring boys. The $4$ girls fill the $4$ gaps in $4! = 24$ ways. By the multiplication principle the number of seatings is $6 \times 24 = 144$.

questions.solution_md: Fix the circular arrangement of one group, then place the other group in the gaps.

questions.stem_md: The number of permutations of $4$ objects from $n$ different objects is $20$ times the number of permutations of $2$ objects from the same $n$, that is $^{n}P_{4} = 20 \times {}^{n}P_{2}$. Determine $n$.
questions.solution_md: Cancel the common factors $n(n - 1)$ and solve the resulting quadratic.

questions.stem_md:
The letters of the word MISSION are arranged in a row. Find the number of distinct arrangements

(a) in all, [1]

(b) in which the two S's are together, [1]

(c) in which the two S's are not together, [1]

(d) that begin with I and end with N. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The word has $7$ letters with I twice and S twice: $\dfrac{7!}{2!\,2!} = 1260$.

(b) Treat SS as one block. The units are SS, M, I, I, O, N: $6$ units with I twice, so $\dfrac{6!}{2!} = 360$.

(c) $1260 - 360 = 900$.

(d) Fix I at the start and N at the end. The remaining letters M, I, S, S, O fill the middle $5$ places: $5$ letters with S twice, so $\dfrac{5!}{2!} = 60$.

questions.solution_md: Block method for (b), complement for (c), end places fixed for (d).

marking_scheme.step: (d) remaining letters M, I, S, S, O

questions.stem_md:
Five-digit numbers are formed from the digits $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$, no digit being used more than once in a number. Find how many numbers

(a) can be formed in all, [1]

(b) are even, [2]

(c) are multiples of $5$, [1]

(d) are greater than $40000$. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The first digit is not $0$: $6$ choices. The other four places take the remaining $6$ digits in order: $^{6}P_{4} = 360$. The number is $6 \times 360 = 2160$.

(b) Units digit $0$: the other four places take the remaining $6$ digits in order, $^{6}P_{4} = 360$. Units digit $2$, $4$ or $6$ ($3$ choices): the first digit is not $0$ and not the units digit, so $5$ choices; the middle three places take the remaining $5$ digits in order, $^{5}P_{3} = 60$. That gives $3 \times 5 \times 60 = 900$. In all $360 + 900 = 1260$.

(c) Units digit $0$ gives $360$. Units digit $5$: the first digit is not $0$ and not $5$, so $5$ choices, and the middle three places take the remaining $5$ digits, $60$ ways: $5 \times 60 = 300$. In all $360 + 300 = 660$.

(d) The first digit is $4$, $5$ or $6$: $3$ choices. The other four places take the remaining $6$ digits: $360$. The number is $3 \times 360 = 1080$.

questions.solution_md: Fix the restricted places first; split on the units digit when $0$ is special.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined school council has to choose a committee of $6$ from $7$ boys and $5$ girls. Find the number of committees

(a) with no restriction, [1]

(b) with exactly $3$ girls, [1]

(c) with at least $4$ boys, [2]

(d) that include one particular boy and one particular girl. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $^{12}C_{6} = 924$.

(b) $3$ girls and $3$ boys: $^{5}C_{3} \times {}^{7}C_{3} = 10 \times 35 = 350$.

(c) At least $4$ boys means $4$ boys and $2$ girls, or $5$ boys and $1$ girl, or $6$ boys. $^{7}C_{4} \times {}^{5}C_{2} = 35 \times 10 = 350$; $^{7}C_{5} \times {}^{5}C_{1} = 21 \times 5 = 105$; $^{7}C_{6} = 7$. The total is $350 + 105 + 7 = 462$.

(d) The two named people are in, so choose the other $4$ from the remaining $10$: $^{10}C_{4} = 210$.

questions.solution_md: Split by the number of boys; for (d) fix the two members and choose the rest.

questions.stem_md:
Eight different people are to sit round a circular table, and seatings that differ only by a rotation count as the same. Find the number of seatings

(a) in all, [1]

(b) in which two named people sit side by side, [1]

(c) in which those two named people do not sit side by side, [1]

(d) in which three named people sit together in a block. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $(8 - 1)! = 5040$.

(b) Treat the two people as one unit: $7$ units round the table in $(7 - 1)! = 720$ ways, and the pair can swap in $2$ ways: $2 \times 720 = 1440$.

(c) $5040 - 1440 = 3600$.

(d) Treat the three people as one block: the block and the other $5$ people make $6$ units, which can be seated in $(6 - 1)! = 120$ ways. The three in the block can be ordered in $3! = 6$ ways. The number is $120 \times 6 = 720$.

questions.solution_md: Circular count: fix the block or the pair as units, then multiply by the order inside the block.

questions.stem_md:
The eight different letters of the word DAUGHTER are used to make arrangements. Find the number of

(a) arrangements of all the letters in a row, [1]

(b) arrangements in which the three vowels are together, [1]

(c) arrangements in which no two vowels are next to each other, [2]

(d) four-letter words, meaningful or not, with exactly two vowels, no letter being repeated. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $8! = 40320$.

(b) Block the vowels A, U, E: the block and the $5$ consonants make $6$ units, $6! = 720$ ways, and the vowels order themselves in $3! = 6$ ways: $720 \times 6 = 4320$.

(c) Arrange the $5$ consonants first: $5! = 120$ ways. They leave $6$ gaps (one before, one after and four between). Place the $3$ vowels in $3$ different gaps in order: $^{6}P_{3} = 120$. The number is $120 \times 120 = 14400$.

(d) Select $2$ of the $3$ vowels and $2$ of the $5$ consonants: $^{3}C_{2} \times {}^{5}C_{2} = 3 \times 10 = 30$. Arrange each set of $4$ letters: $4! = 24$. The number of words is $30 \times 24 = 720$.

questions.solution_md: Block for (b); consonants first and vowels in the gaps for (c); select then arrange for (d).

marking_scheme.step: (c) consonants $5!$ and $6$ gaps for the vowels

questions.stem_md:
A school has $10$ different story books and will give $4$ of them as prizes. Among the books is one particular atlas-story called Book Z. Find the number of ways of choosing the $4$ books

(a) with no restriction, [1]

(b) so that Book Z is included, [1]

questions.stem_md:
(a) Derive the formula $^{n}P_{r} = \dfrac{n!}{(n - r)!}$ for the number of arrangements of $r$ objects chosen from $n$ different objects. [2]

(b) Hence deduce the formula for $^{n}C_{r}$. [1]

(c) Show that $^{n}C_{r} = \dfrac{n - r + 1}{r} \times {}^{n}C_{r-1}$, and use it with $^{12}C_{4} = 495$ to find $^{12}C_{5}$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Fill $r$ places one after another. The first place can be filled in $n$ ways, the second in $n - 1$ ways, and so on, until the $r$-th place, which can be filled in $n - r + 1$ ways. By the multiplication principle $^{n}P_{r} = n(n - 1)(n - 2)\cdots(n - r + 1)$. Multiplying and dividing by $(n - r)!$ gives $^{n}P_{r} = \dfrac{n!}{(n - r)!}$.

(b) Each selection of $r$ objects can be arranged in $r!$ ways, so $^{n}P_{r} = r! \times {}^{n}C_{r}$. Hence $^{n}C_{r} = \dfrac{^{n}P_{r}}{r!} = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n - r)!}$.

(c) $\dfrac{^{n}C_{r}}{^{n}C_{r-1}} = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n - r)!} \times \dfrac{(r - 1)!\,(n - r + 1)!}{n!} = \dfrac{n - r + 1}{r}$, since $r! = r\,(r - 1)!$ and $(n - r + 1)! = (n - r + 1)(n - r)!$. For $n = 12$ and $r = 5$: $^{12}C_{5} = \dfrac{12 - 5 + 1}{5} \times 495 = \dfrac{8}{5} \times 495 = 792$.
